children.text: The grounds of the National Shrine of the Divine Mercy in Marilao, Bulacan, hold a Divine Mercy statue about 30 m (100 ft) tall. It is about an hour from Manila by NLEX, which makes it a good half-day pilgrimage and photo trip.

Marilao is a city at the southern edge of Bulacan, north of Manila, on the route of NLEX and MacArthur Highway toward northern Luzon. The National Shrine and Parish of the Divine Mercy, on a hill in Barangay Santa Rosa I, is the city's most conspicuous Catholic pilgrimage site. It is a parish of the Diocese of Malolos, and the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) elevated it to national shrine status. According to Wikipedia, the first Mass was held on February 2, 1992, and the church was completed and consecrated in November 1994.

The shrine's symbol is the Divine Mercy statue on its grounds. Jesus, dressed in white, raises his right hand in blessing and points with his left hand toward the light at his chest, based on the "Vilnius image" drawn from the vision St. Faustina Kowalska described. The statue itself is about 30.48 m (100 ft) tall, and with the roughly 15.24 m (50 ft) building that serves as its base the whole structure reaches about 45.7 m (150 ft). Construction began in January 2016, and it was unveiled and blessed on January 19, 2017, during the 4th World Apostolic Congress on Mercy (WACOM). The idea is credited to the Filipino priest Fr. Prospero Tenorio. The statue is said to have been 3D-printed in sections and then coated in fiberglass for weatherproofing. The base building contains a multipurpose hall and dormitory facilities. When it was unveiled it was the tallest Divine Mercy statue in the Philippines, but there are records of a larger one later built in Calbiga, Samar, so "largest in the world" is best read as promotional wording. It is enough to remember that it is among the largest in the Philippines.

This is not an amusement-park attraction but a parish where Masses are still held, so respecting the atmosphere matters more than how long you stay. On the other hand, there is no admission fee and it is quiet, which suits anyone near Manila who wants a calm half day, Catholic families, and people who like photographing large monuments. Below we go through the layout of the grounds, how to get there, costs and cautions in order. One thing to know before you go: there are several "Divine Mercy" sites around the Philippines, including the Divine Mercy hill in El Salvador, Misamis Oriental, the one in Toledo, Cebu, and the large statue in Calbiga, Samar, so typing only "Divine Mercy" into a map app can send you to the wrong place. This guide covers the national shrine in Barangay Santa Rosa I, Marilao, Bulacan, so entering "National Shrine of the Divine Mercy, Marilao" in your navigation app is the most accurate.

Overall you can see the shrine in two to three hours, and it combines well in a single day with other Bulacan churches and historic sites north of Manila. Obando, Meycauayan and Malolos are all in the same province, so you can build a day-long church-pilgrimage route. But too many stops will wear you out in NLEX traffic, so add only one or two other places to the shrine.

blocks.title: Divine Mercy statue, about 30 m tall

children.text: This is the shrine's biggest sight. It can be seen from far across Marilao, and standing close, the white statue fills the sky above its base building. The white shows clearly in morning light, while afternoon shots tend to be backlit.

Consecrated in 1994, the church keeps an image of the Merciful Jesus near the altar. Worshippers have priority during services, so look around quietly from the back and avoid taking photos during Mass.

According to Wikipedia, the church basement holds a chapel with a replica of the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, and worshippers sometimes bottle the flowing water to take home. It is a place of faith, so be careful with photos and conversation.

blocks.title: Calvary and the Stations of the Cross

children.text: On the hill behind the church are the 14 Stations of the Cross, made of life-sized sculptures. Many pilgrims walk here during Holy Week, and at other times it is a quiet place for a stroll.

blocks.title: Rosary Hill and the grotto chapels

children.text: The grounds include Rosary Hill, the Grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes and the Grotto of the Resurrection. Wikipedia says people come here to pray for good health. There are steps, so comfortable shoes help.

It is said to include replicas of the former home of John Paul II, St. Faustina's convent chapel in Vilnius, and the Auschwitz cell where St. Maximilian Kolbe was held. Opening hours may not be fixed, so confirm locally.
An auditorium where Mass is also held when worshippers overflow on Sundays. It also gives a sense of how crowded the grounds get on big feast days.

In Divine Mercy devotion, 3 p.m. is remembered as the hour Jesus died, and the prayer of mercy is offered then. According to visitor guides, prayers of mercy are said at 3 p.m. at this shrine too, so those interested in the faith may want to time their visit accordingly.

items.title: Half-day course from Manila
items.subtitle: A route that avoids the morning Mass hours

children.text: Set out from Manila (Quezon City or the Monumento area). By car or taxi allow about
1 hour
, and assume more during rush hour.
Arrive in Marilao and park near the shrine entrance or get off the tricycle. First take photos of the whole statue from a distance.
Look around the church and the Guadalupe Chapel in the basement quietly. If Mass is on, a brief stay at the back is enough.
Walk the Calvary and Stations of the Cross, Rosary Hill and the grotto chapels behind the church. The sun is strong, so bring a hat and water.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant, then move on to the Obando shrine or Meycauayan if you wish.
The shrine's official Mass times differ between weekdays and Sundays, and special schedules apply during Holy Week and on Divine Mercy Sunday. Check the shrine's announcements before you leave.

items.title: 3 p.m. Hour of Mercy course
items.subtitle: A visit timed to the prayer hour

children.text: Eat lunch and set out for Marilao. Parking is hard on Sunday afternoons, so it is better to arrive early.
Walk the grounds slowly and view the statue from different angles.
Join quietly, or simply watch, the prayer of mercy in the church or at the outdoor prayer area.
As the sun gets lower, warm light touches the statue, so it is a good time for photos once more.

items.title: From Manila by car or taxi

children.text: Take NLEX to the Marilao exit, then follow the shrine signs onto M. Villarica Road. Guides say it takes about
1 hour
from north Manila, though it varies greatly with traffic.
If you use Grab or a taxi, fares vary by time of day and starting point, so check in the app first. It can be hard to find a ride back, so arranging a round-trip hire in advance is convenient.

items.title: From Manila by bus or jeepney

children.text: From the Monumento (Caloocan) area, take a bus or jeepney toward Marilao along MacArthur Highway. It is described as taking about
1 hour
, but longer during congested hours.
In Marilao town, take a tricycle and say "Divine Mercy" and the driver will take you to the shrine. Fares depend on distance and negotiation, so confirm before you ride.
Bus routes and fares change often, so confirm locally.
If you come from abroad, land at Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), pass through Manila and head north on NLEX. From the airport to the shrine, it is safest to allow about
1.5–2 hours
by car.

In the November–May dry season the Stations of the Cross and Rosary Hill are comfortable to walk and photos come out sharp. From March to May, though, the midday sun is strong and there is little shade, so early morning or late afternoon is better.

During Divine Mercy Sunday (the first Sunday after Easter) and Holy Week, many pilgrims come and parking and Mass seating get very crowded. If you want quiet, we recommend a weekday morning. Showers are frequent in the June–October rainy season, so bring an umbrella.

The shrine is a half-day trip, so few people stay overnight in Marilao. You can make a day trip from Manila, or use city hotels toward Malolos or Meycauayan in Bulacan. Room rates and availability change often, so check a booking app.

For meals, use the small restaurants around the shrine and the fast-food places in Marilao town. Bulacan is known for snacks such as pastillas (milk candy) and egg pie, so try them if you are also visiting Obando, Meycauayan and Malolos on the same day. Eating inside the shrine may be restricted, so follow the posted rules.
The pilgrims' center and dormitory facilities in the shrine appear to be used mainly for church groups and events. Ask the shrine office whether ordinary tourists can stay and at what rate.
The shrine is a parish church. Wear clothes that cover shoulders and knees, and avoid swimwear, sleeveless tops and short shorts.
Do not use flash during Mass, and keep your voice down. Ask permission before taking photos inside the church.
Guides say the time around the 6:30 a.m. weekday Mass is the quietest. If you mostly want photos, 9–10 a.m. is also good.
On Sundays and big feast days the parking lot fills up. Go early or take a tricycle from town.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water. The grounds have steps and slopes, so wear comfortable shoes.
Mass and confession times differ between weekdays and Sundays and can change. Calling or emailing the shrine office is the most accurate way to check.
Whether the base building is open varies by day. If you plan to go inside, confirm locally.
Keep an eye on your belongings among the pilgrims. Watch for pickpockets during big events.
The shrine's Mass, office and building opening hours change in Holy Week and on Divine Mercy Sunday. Check the latest announcements before you visit.
This is a place of faith, so avoid revealing clothes and loud voices.
NLEX and Marilao town are very congested during rush hours. Leave generous time for the return trip too.
There is no official admission fee, but sellers of religious items and candles may approach you. Decline politely if you do not need them.
If someone who offers to guide you unasked demands money, refuse firmly.
Prepare water, an umbrella and a light jacket for rainy-season showers and midday heat.
A shrine a short drive from Marilao, famous for a dance procession each May in which people pray for fertility. It makes a good pilgrimage route to combine on the same day.
An old city in southern Bulacan where you can see a Spanish-era church and local living heritage.
The central church of the Diocese of Malolos, to which Marilao belongs. You can head north from Marilao to see it.
A historic church where the Malolos Congress met in 1899, where you can learn the story of the First Philippine Republic.
